facts.claim: Cain defines shyness as the fear of social disapproval or humiliation, and introversion as a preference for environments that are not over-stimulating; she uses this to show the two can be separated.
Examples of the split: Barbra Streisand as a shy extrovert (outgoing but with severe stage fright), Bill Gates as a non-shy introvert.

Jerome Kagan of Harvard started a study in 1989 with about 500 four-month-old infants, exposing them for forty-five minutes to taped voices, popping balloons, colorful mobiles and cotton swabs with the smell of alcohol.

Kagan called infants who pumped their limbs and cried 'high-reactive' and calm ones 'low-reactive'; high-reactives were later more likely to become quiet, introverted children, low-reactives relaxed, confident extroverts.
Kagan retested the children with new things (a clown, a woman in a gas mask) at ages two, four, seven and eleven; most matched his predictions.
Kagan stressed that high and low reactivity were not the only routes to introversion and extroversion.
Cain went to Harvard Business School, which she calls the 'Spiritual Capital of Extroversion', where future leaders are taught to act confidently and make decisions with incomplete information.

At HBS classroom participation drives status and grades; each incoming cohort runs the Subarctic Survival Situation, a group exercise in which students brainstorm how to survive a cold-weather crash with limited resources.

Students attend largely to build lasting personal networks; days are group exercises and the evenings are 'an extreme sport'. Asked whether anyone on campus is quieter, one student answered 'I couldn't tell you'.
Cain argues that introverts prefer to work independently and that solitude can be a catalyst to innovation; brainstorming in groups is less effective than assumed.

Adam Grant's pizza-franchise leadership study appears in Quiet: extroverted leaders do better with passive employees, introverted leaders with proactive ones (figures reported as 16% and 14% higher profits, unverified in primary text).
By one reviewer's account, about a quarter of Kagan's high-reactive children apparently suffered from social anxiety disorder.
Carl Schwartz, who retested the children as adults, concluded that we can stretch our personalities, but only up to a point.
Per studies Cain cites, one third to one half of Americans are introverts; introverts and extroverts have the same average IQ, but introverts tend to earn better grades in high school and college.
Cain cites financial executives who said cautious, introverted leaders on Wall Street might have noticed warning signs before the economic meltdown (their view, not a study result).
Cain calls the trend of group work in schools and offices the New Groupthink and says group work should not dominate the school day.

rejected.claim: Introvert and extrovert babies; extrovert babies 'curious and calm'; introverts have a 'neurological preference, not a character weakness'
rejected.reason: Curious/calm wording and the neurological framing not found in sources; used only Kagan's reported reactions.

rejected.claim: A faculty member told Cain: 'If you have an idea but don't say it, you don't have an idea.'
Anatoly Karpov as a quiet chess champion
rejected.reason: Not found in any Quiet summary.

rejected.claim: Buffett, Gates, Einstein as one list of deep thinkers
rejected.reason: Gates appears (f2); the list as framed is not verified.

rejected.claim: Adam Grant found ambiverts are the best salespeople; introverted salespeople are better in some categories (1413)
rejected.reason: Grant's sales study is a 2013 paper (Psychological Science, 340 call-centre reps), after Quiet (2012); not shown to be in the book.

rejected.claim: Introverts are better listeners who shape the solution to the customer's need
rejected.reason: Not found in the book's sales material.
